'''Omar Mwannes Yaghi''' ({{langx|ar| عمر مُؤنس ياغي}}; born February 9, 1965) is a chemist{{Efn|Yaghi was born into a [[Palestinian refugee]] family in [[Amman]], Jordan. When he was 15, he moved to the United States and he received Saudi citizenship in 2021. He holds Jordanian, United States, and Saudi Arabian citizenships.<ref>{{Cite news |date=October 9, 2025 |title=Four Arab countries claim Nobel chemistry laureate Omar Yaghi as their own, despite controversy over past Israel link |url=https://www.newarab.com/news/arab-countries-claim-nobel-prize-winner-omar-yaghi-their-own |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251107070144/https://www.newarab.com/news/arab-countries-claim-nobel-prize-winner-omar-yaghi-their-own |archive-date=November 7, 2025 |access-date=February 10, 2026 |work=[[The New Arab]]}}</ref>}} best known for developing [[Metal–organic framework|metal–organic frameworks]] (MOFs) and pioneering [[Reticular materials|reticular chemistry]]. He was awarded the 2025 [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]], shared with [[Richard Robson (chemist)|Richard Robson]] and [[Susumu Kitagawa]], for this work.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2025 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2025/press-release/ |access-date=2025-10-08 |website=NobelPrize.org |language=en-US}}</ref>

From 2012 to 2026, Yaghi was a University Professor and James and Neeltje Tretter Endowed Chair in Chemistry at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. In July 2026, he left the university to lead a newly-established artificial intelligence and material science research institute at [[Tsinghua University]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ahart |first=Jenna |last2=Basu |first2=Mohana |date=2026-07-08 |title=Nobel-winning chemist leaves US to direct AI materials lab in China |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-02143-x |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=655 |issue=8123 |pages=551–552 |doi=10.1038/d41586-026-02143-x |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Analysts and media outlets characterized the move as a significant indicator of shifting geopolitical dynamics in scientific research, driven by factors such as changing federal funding structures in the [[United States]] and expanded institutional recruitment initiatives by [[China]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-07-04 |title=Nobel-winning scientist Omar Yaghi joins China’s Tsinghua University from the US |url=https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/article/3359430/nobel-prize-winning-materials-scientist-omar-yaghi-joins-tsinghua-university-us |access-date=2026-07-10 |website=South China Morning Post |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ahart |first=Jenna |last2=Basu |first2=Mohana |date=2026-07-08 |title=Nobel-winning chemist leaves US to direct AI materials lab in China |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-02143-x |journal=Nature |language=en |doi=10.1038/d41586-026-02143-x |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Yaghi is also an affiliate scientist at [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]], founding director of the Berkeley Global Science Institute, and a member of the U.S. [[National Academy of Sciences]]<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20190430143122/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2019-nas-election.html " National Academy of Sciences Elects Members and Foreign Associates "], ''[[National Academy of Sciences]]'', Retrieved on 30 April 2019.</ref> and the [[German National Academy of Sciences Leopoldina]].<ref>[http://www.leopoldina.org/en/members/list-of-members/list-of-members/member/Member/show/omar-yaghi/ " List of Members Expert Search Professor Dr. Omar M. Yaghi "], ''[[German National Academy of Sciences Leopoldina]] "]'', Retrieved on 9 June 2023.</ref><ref>[https://chemistry.berkeley.edu/news/omar-yaghi-appointed-university-professor " Omar Yaghi appointed as University Professor "], ''[[UC Berkeley College of Chemistry]] "]'', Retrieved on 26 June 2025.</ref> In January 2025, he became the seventh president of the [[World Cultural Council]], an international organization promoting cultural and scientific advancement.<ref>[https://www.consejoculturalmundial.org/our-president/ " Our President "], ''[[World Cultural Council]]'', Retrieved on 25 July 2025.</ref>

livestock.<ref>[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bzM_qeOumss "A Pioneer in Reticular Chemistry: Shaping a Sustainable Future – Omar M. At the age of 15, encouraged by his father, he moved to the United States.<ref>[https://www.forbesmiddleeast.com/en/the-alchemist/ " The Alchemist "] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180828030715/https://www.forbesmiddleeast.com/en/the-alchemist/ |date=2018-08-28 }}, ''[[Forbes]]'', Retrieved on 1 February 2018.</ref> Although he knew little English, he began classes at [[Hudson Valley Community College]]. He graduated in 1983 with an Associate of Science in Mathematics and Science.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=HVCC, UAlbany Alum Omar Yaghi Shares 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry {{!}} HVCC |url=https://www.hvcc.edu/about/news/archives/2025/10/hvcc-ualbany-alum-omar-yaghi-shares-2025-nobel-prize-in-chemistry.html |access-date=2025-12-24 |website=www.hvcc.edu |language=en-US}}</ref> He then transferred to the [[State University of New York at Albany]], where he completed his Chemistry Bachelor of Science degree in 1985.<ref name=":1" /> He pursued his graduate studies at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]], earning his PhD in 1990 under the guidance of [[Walter G. Klemperer]].<ref>{{cite thesis |title=Synthesis, structure, and reactivity of polyoxovanadates in nonaqueous media |year=1990 |degree=PhD |institution=[[University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign]] |last=Yaghi |first=Omar M. |id={{ProQuest|303854222}} |oclc=774917622}}</ref> He then served as a [[National Science Foundation]] postdoctoral fellow at [[Harvard University]] (1990–1992) under [[Richard H. Holm]]. In July 2026 he moved to [[Tsinghua University]], China, as full time  Chair Professor. He had been an Honorary Professor there since 2022 and a Foreign Member of the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]] since 2025.<ref>{{cite web |title=Nobel Laureate in Chemistry Omar M. Yaghi joins Tsinghua University full-time |url=https://www.tsinghua.edu.cn/en/info/1244/14984.htm |website=Tsinghua University |publisher=Tsinghua University |access-date=8 July 2026}}</ref><ref name="CASAD">{{cite web |title=Foreign Members of CASAD |url=https://english.casad.cas.cn/newsroom/ma/202607/t20260708_1176835.html |website=Academic Divisions of the Chinese Academy of Sciences |publisher=Academic Divisions of the Chinese Academy of Sciences |access-date=8 July 2026}}</ref>

In 2021, Yaghi was granted Saudi citizenship by royal [[decree]].<ref name=":0">{{cite web|url=https://www.arabnews.com/node/1967886/saudi-arabia |title=Internationally renowned chemist Omar Yaghi 'honored to accept Saudi citizenship' |website=arabnews.com |date=14 November 2021}}</ref>

== Academic career ==
Yaghi began his academic career as an assistant professor at [[Arizona State University]] (1992–1998). He then held the Robert W. Parry Professorship of Chemistry at the [[University of Michigan]] (1999–2006), followed by the [[Christopher S. Foote]] Professorship of Chemistry and the Irving and Jean Stone Chair in Physical Sciences at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] (2007–2012).<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/anie.201802237 | doi=10.1002/anie.201802237 | title=Wolf Prize in Chemistry: M. Fujita and O. M. Yaghi / Albrecht Kossel Prize: A. Beck-Sickinger | journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition | date=2018 | volume=57 | issue=13 | page=3287 | pmid=29504702 | bibcode=2018ACIE...57.3287. | url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In 2012, he moved to the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he was the James and Neeltje Tretter Professor of Chemistry. From 2012 to 2013, he served as the director of the [[Molecular Foundry]] at the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]]. He is the Founding Director of the Berkeley Global Science Institute and a co-director of the [[Kavli Foundation (United States)#Nanoscience|Kavli Energy NanoSciences Institute]], a partnership between UC Berkeley and the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. He also co-directs the California Research Alliance by [[BASF]] and the Bakar Institute of Digital Materials for the Planet.<ref>[https://data.berkeley.edu/news/new-institute-brings-together-chemistry-and-machine-learning-tackle-climate-change " New institute brings together chemistry and machine learning to tackle climate change "], Retrieved on 21 September 2022.</ref>

In May 2025, the University of California Board of Regents promoted Yaghi to the rank of University Professor, the system's highest honor reserved for scholars of the highest international distinction.<ref>[https://chemistry.berkeley.edu/news/omar-yaghi-appointed-university-professor " Omar Yaghi appointed as University Professor "], ''[[UC Berkeley College of Chemistry]]'', Retrieved on 25 July 2025.</ref>

In July 2026, Yaghi vacated his position at UC Berkeley to launch the Yaghi Science Initiative and to take up a position at [[Tsinghua University]] in China, to lead an [[artificial intelligence]] laboratory dedicated to accelerating the discovery of new materials.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kaye |first=John E. |date=2026-07-03 |title=Nobel laureate Omar Yaghi launches global science network |url=https://the-european.eu/story-62714/nobel-laureate-omar-yaghi-launches-global-science-network.html |access-date=2026-08-10 |website=The European Magazine |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-07-04 |title=Nobel-winning scientist Omar Yaghi joins China’s Tsinghua University from the US |url=https://www.scmp.com/news/china/science/article/3359430/nobel-prize-winning-materials-scientist-omar-yaghi-joins-tsinghua-university-us |access-date=2026-07-05 |website=South China Morning Post |language=en}}</ref>

== Research ==
=== Reticular chemistry ===
{{See also|Reticular materials}}

Yaghi is the pioneer of reticular chemistry, a field dedicated to assembling molecular building blocks into open, crystalline frameworks using strong bonds.<ref>[https://cen.acs.org/articles/95/i28/Omar-Yaghi-wins-Albert-Einstein.html " Omar Yaghi wins Albert Einstein World Award of Science "], ''[[Chemical & Engineering News]]'', 10 July 2017. Retrieved on 12 March 2018.</ref><ref>[https://cen.acs.org/articles/96/web/2018/02/Makoto-Fujita-and-Omar-Yaghi-win-Wolf-Prize-in-Chemistry.html " Makoto Fujita and Omar Yaghi win Wolf Prize in Chemistry "], '' Chemical & Engineering News'', 19 February 2018. Retrieved on 12 March 2018.</ref><ref>[http://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2017/fd/c7fd00160f#!divAbstract " Spiers Memorial Lecture – Progress and prospects of reticular chemistry "], ''[[Royal Society of Chemistry]]'', 18 August 2017. Retrieved on 12 March 2018.</ref>

According to the International [[Balzan Prize]] Foundation, Yaghi first proposed using molecular building blocks and strong bonds to form crystalline materials in the early 1990s. At the time, the scientific community considered this idea chemically unfeasible, as such syntheses typically resulted in non-crystalline, amorphous solids. However, in 1995, Yaghi successfully crystallized metal-organic structures in which metal ions are connected by charged organic linkers, such as [[carboxylate]]s, via strong bonds. This breakthrough led to the development of a new class of materials known as [[metal–organic framework]]s (MOFs), marking the birth of reticular chemistry.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.balzan.org/en/materiali-nanoporosi-per-applicazioni-ambientali |title=Omar M. Yaghi 2024 Balzan Prize for Nanoporous Materials for Environmental Applications |work=Fondazione Internazionale Premio Balzan |publisher=International Balzan Prize Foundation |date=November 22, 2024 |access-date=December 25, 2024 |archive-date=April 18, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250418130633/https://www.balzan.org/en/materiali-nanoporosi-per-applicazioni-ambientali |url-status=dead }}</ref>

=== Metal-organic frameworks ===
{{Primary sources|section|date=October 2025}}

Yaghi's most recognized work is in the design, synthesis, application, and popularization of [[Metal–organic framework|metal–organic frameworks]] (MOFs). According to IUPAC, MOFs are a subclass of [[coordination polymer]]s, a category first reported in 1959.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kinoshita |first1=Yukio |last2=Matsubara |first2=Ikuo |last3=Higuchi |first3=Taiichi |last4=Saito |first4=Yoshihiko |date=1959-11-01 |title=The Crystal Structure of Bis(adiponitrilo)copper(I) Nitrate |url=https://doi.org/10.1246/bcsj.32.1221 |journal=Bulletin of the Chemical Society of Japan |volume=32 |issue=11 |pages=1221–1226 |doi=10.1246/bcsj.32.1221 |issn=0009-2673|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Earlier work included E. A. Tomic's 1965 study on the thermal stability of various coordination polymers<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tomic |first=E. A. |date=1965 |title=Thermal stability of coordination polymers |url=https://doi.org/10.1002/app.1965.070091121 |journal=Journal of Applied Polymer Science |volume=9 |issue=11 |pages=3745–3752 |doi=10.1002/app.1965.070091121 |bibcode=1965JAPS....9.3745T |url-access=subscription }}</ref> and the work of Hoskins and [[Richard Robson (chemist)|Richard Robson]] in 1989 on a 3D coordination polymer structure.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hoskins |first1=Bernard F. |last2=Robson |first2=Richard |date=July 1989 |title=Infinite polymeric frameworks consisting of three dimensionally linked rod-like segments |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00197a079 |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |volume=111 |issue=15 |pages=5962–5964 |doi=10.1021/ja00197a079 |bibcode=1989JAChS.111.5962H |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Robson |first=R. |date=2008-09-23 |title=Design and its limitations in the construction of bi- and poly-nuclear coordination complexes and coordination polymers (aka MOFs): a personal view |url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2008/dt/b805617j |journal=Dalton Transactions |issue=38 |pages=5113–5131 |doi=10.1039/B805617J |pmid=18813362 |issn=1477-9234|url-access=subscription }}</ref> However, these early coordination polymers were typically frail, disordered structures with poorly defined properties.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.kva.se/en/news/arets-aminoffpris-till-grundarna-av-natverkskemin-2/ |title=This year's Aminoff Prize goes to the founders of reticular chemistry |date=September 13, 2018}}</ref>

In the 1990s, Yaghi made three key breakthroughs that transformed fragile coordination polymers into the architecturally robust, permanently porous MOFs in use today:

#The crystallization of metal-organic structures using strong bonds between metal ions and charged organic linkers like carboxylates (1995).<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Yaghi, O. M. |author2=Li, G. |author3=Li, H. |title= Selective binding and removal of guests in a microporous metal–organic framework |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|date=1995|volume=378|issue= 6558|pages=703–706 |doi=10.1038/378703a0|bibcode=1995Natur.378..703Y }}</ref>
#The introduction of metal-carboxylate clusters as secondary building units (SBUs), which enabled robust frameworks with permanent porosity, later confirmed by gas adsorption isotherms (1998).<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Li, H. |author2=Eddaoudi, M. |author3=Groy, T. L. |author4=Yaghi, O. M. |title=Establishing Microporosity in Open Metal-Organic Frameworks: Gas Sorption Isotherms for Zn (BDC)(BDC= 1,4-Benzenedicarboxylate)|journal=[[Journal of the American Chemical Society]]|date=1998|volume=120|issue=33|pages=8571–8572|doi=10.1021/ja981669x }}</ref>
#The realization of ultra-high porosity with [[MOF-5]] (1999).<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Li, H. |author2=Eddaoudi, M. |author3=O’Keeffee, M. |author4=Yaghi, O. M. |title=Design and synthesis of an exceptionally stable and highly porous metal-organic framework |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|date=1999|volume=402|issue=6759|pages=276–279|doi=10.1038/46248 |bibcode=1999Natur.402..276L |hdl=2027.42/62847 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

The strong bonds in MOFs are fundamental to their structural robustness, ultra-high porosity, and longevity in industrial applications.

=== Covalent organic frameworks ===
{{Primary sources|section|date=October 2025}}

In 2005, Omar M. Yaghi published the seminal paper on [[covalent organic framework]]s (COFs), reporting the first series of 2D COFs.<ref>{{Cite journal | url= https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1120411 | title= Porous, Crystalline, Covalent Organic Frameworks | date=November 18, 2005| doi= 10.1126/science.1120411 | last1= CôTé | first1= Adrien P. | last2= Benin | first2= Annabelle I. | last3= Ockwig | first3= Nathan W. | last4= O'Keeffe | first4= Michael | last5= Matzger | first5= Adam J. | last6= Yaghi | first6= Omar M. | journal= Science | volume= 310 | issue= 5751 | pages= 1166–1170 | pmid= 16293756 | bibcode= 2005Sci...310.1166C | url-access= subscription }}</ref> This work demonstrated the design and synthesis of COFs via condensation reactions of {{ill|1,4-benzenediboronic acid|zh|1,4-苯二硼酸}} ({{chem2|''p''\-C6H4[B(OH)2]2}}) and [[hexahydroxytriphenylene|2,3,6,7,10,11-hexahydroxytriphenylene]] ({{chem2|C18H6(OH)6}}). Powder X-ray diffraction of the highly crystalline products—with [[empirical formulas]] {{chem2|(C3H2BO)6*(C9H12)1}} (COF-1) and {{chem2|C9H4BO2}} (COF-5)—revealed 2D expanded porous graphitic layers with either [[staggered conformation|staggered]] (COF-1) or [[eclipsed conformation|eclipsed]] (COF-5) structures. These architectures are held together by strong covalent bonds between boron, carbon, and oxygen atoms, creating rigid porous structures with pore sizes ranging from 7 to 27 [[Angstrom|ångströms]]. COF-1 and COF-5 exhibit high thermal stability (up to 500–600 °C), permanent porosity, and high surface areas of 711 and 1590 square meters per gram, respectively.<ref>{{Cite journal | url= https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1120411 | title= Porous, Crystalline, Covalent Organic Frameworks | date=November 18, 2005| doi= 10.1126/science.1120411 | last1= CôTé | first1= Adrien P. | last2= Benin | first2= Annabelle I. | last3= Ockwig | first3= Nathan W. | last4= O'Keeffe | first4= Michael | last5= Matzger | first5= Adam J. | last6= Yaghi | first6= Omar M. | journal= Science | volume= 310 | issue= 5751 | pages= 1166–1170 | pmid= 16293756 | bibcode= 2005Sci...310.1166C | url-access= subscription }}</ref>

The synthesis of 3D COFs had been hindered by longstanding practical and conceptual challenges until Yaghi's group first achieved it in 2007.<ref>{{Cite journal|doi = 10.1126/science.1139915|title = Designed Synthesis of 3D Covalent Organic Frameworks|year = 2007|last1 = El-Kaderi|first1 = H. M.|last2 = Hunt|first2 = J. R.|last3 = Mendoza-Cortes|first3 = J. L.|last4 = Cote|first4 = A. P.|last5 = Taylor|first5 = R. E.|last6 = O'Keeffe|first6 = M.|last7 = Yaghi|first7 = O. M.|journal = Science|volume = 316|issue = 5822|pages = 268–272|pmid = 17431178|bibcode = 2007Sci...316..268E|s2cid = 19555677| url=https://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechAUTHORS:20130520-133655834 }}</ref>

Yaghi also pioneered the design and production of [[zeolitic imidazolate framework]]s (ZIFs). MOFs, COFs, and ZIFs are renowned for their extreme properties, such as very high surface areas (e.g., {{val|5640|u=m<sup>2</sup>/g}} for MOF-177)<ref>{{cite journal|author1=A.G. Wong-Foy|author2=A.J. Matzger|author3=O.M. Yaghi|year=2006|title=Exceptional H<sub>2</sub> Saturation Uptake in Microporous Metal-Organic Frameworks|journal=[[Journal of the American Chemical Society]]|volume=128|issue=11|pages=3494–3495|doi=10.1021/ja058213h|pmid=16536503}}</ref> and very low crystalline densities (e.g., {{val|0.17|u=g·cm<sup>−3</sup>}} for COF-108).<ref>{{cite journal|author1=H.M. El-Kaderi|author2=J.R. Hunt|author3=J.L. Mendoza-Cortes|author4=A.P. Côté|author5=R.E. Taylor|author6=M. O'Keeffe|author7=O.M. Yaghi|year=2007|title=Designed Synthesis of 3D Covalent Organic Frameworks|url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/38578/7/El-Kaderi.SOM.revised.pdf|journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]]|volume=316|issue=5822|pages=268–272|bibcode=2007Sci...316..268E|doi=10.1126/science.1139915|pmid=17431178|s2cid=19555677}}</ref>

=== Molecular weaving ===
[[File:Molecular Weaving.png|thumb|Molecular weaving<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Yuzhong |last2=Ma |first2=Yanhang |last3=Zhao |first3=Yingbo |last4=Sun |first4=Xixi |last5=Gándara |first5=Felipe |last6=Furukawa |first6=Hiroyasu |last7=Liu |first7=Zheng |last8=Zhu |first8=Hanyu |last9=Zhu |first9=Chenhui |last10=Suenaga |first10=Kazutomo |last11=Oleynikov |first11=Peter |last12=Alshammari |first12=Ahmad S. |last13=Zhang |first13=Xiang |last14=Terasaki |first14=Osamu |last15=Yaghi |first15=Omar M. |date=2016-01-22 |title=Weaving of organic threads into a crystalline covalent organic framework |journal=Science |volume=351 |issue=6271 |pages=365–369 |doi=10.1126/science.aad4011 |issn=1095-9203 |pmid=26798010|bibcode=2016Sci...351..365L }}</ref>|150x150px]]
Yaghi pioneered the field of molecular weaving, achieving the first synthesis of a material (COF-505) woven at the atomic and molecular levels.<ref>[https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aad4011 " Weaving of organic threads into a crystalline covalent organic framework "], ''[[Science (journal)]]'', Retrieved on 16 June 2019.</ref><ref>[https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/01/160121185624.htm " First materials woven at atomic and molecular levels: Weaving a new story for COFs and MOFs "], ''[[ScienceDaily]]'', Retrieved on 16 June 2019.</ref>

He has led efforts to apply reticular materials in clean energy technologies, including hydrogen and methane storage,<ref>[http://pubs.acs.org/cen/topstory/8003/8003notw1.html " Crystal Sponges "], ''Chemical & Engineering News '', 21 January 2002. Retrieved on 12 March 2018.</ref><ref>[http://pubs.acs.org/cen/topstory/8120/8120notw1.html " Porous Crystals Soak Up Hydrogen "], ''Chemical & Engineering News'', 19 May 2003. Retrieved on 12 March 2018.</ref> carbon dioxide capture,<ref>[https://www.technologyreview.com/s/409547/a-better-way-to-capture-carbon/ " A Better Way to Capture Carbon "], ''[[MIT Technology Review]]'', 15 February 2008. Retrieved on 12 March 2018.</ref><ref>[https://www.chemistryworld.com/news/super-sized-molecular-sponges-boost-carbon-capture/3003830.article " Super-sized molecular sponges boost carbon capture "], ''[[Chemistry World]]'', 7 May 2008. Retrieved on 12 March 2018.</ref> and harvesting water from desert air using low{{nbhyph}}grade heat.<ref>[https://www.science.org/content/article/new-solar-powered-device-can-pull-water-straight-desert-air " This new solar-powered device can pull water straight from the desert air "], ''[[Science Magazine]]'', April 13, 2017. Retrieved on March 10, 2018.</ref><ref name="duncan-2026">
{{cite news
 | last1 = Duncan | first1 = Natricia
 | title = 'Reimagining matter': Nobel laureate invents machine that harvests water from dry air
 | date = 21 February 2026
 | work = The Guardian
 | location = London, United Kingdom
 | issn = 0261-3077
 | url = https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/feb/21/nobel-laureate-omar-yaghi-invents-machine-that-harvests-water-from-dry-air
 | access-date = 2026-02-21
}}
</ref>

According to a [[Thomson Reuters]] analysis, Yaghi was the world's second-most-cited chemist between 2000 and 2010.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Top 100 Chemists, 2000–2010 – |url=http://archive.sciencewatch.com/dr/sci/misc/Top100Chemists2000-10/|access-date=2022-02-03|website=ScienceWatch.com}}</ref>

== Entrepreneurship ==
In 2020, Yaghi founded Atoco, a California-based startup focused on commercializing his advancements in MOF and COF technologies for [[Carbon capture and storage|carbon capture]] and [[Atmospheric water generator|atmospheric water harvesting]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-01-12 |title=Founder, Prof. Omar Yaghi: "From Desert to Discovery: The Journey of Reticular Chemistry" |url=https://atoco.com/blogs/from-desert-to-discovery-the-journey-of-reticular-chemistry/ |access-date=2024-04-29 |website=Atoco }}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |date=2023-09-08 |title=A World Renowned Chemist Wants to Suck Water, and Carbon, Out of the Air |url=https://time.com/6312091/chemist-omar-yaghi-is-on-a-quest-to-eliminate-water-scarcity/ |access-date=2024-04-29 |magazine=Time |archive-date=2025-06-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250617132507/https://time.com/6312091/chemist-omar-yaghi-is-on-a-quest-to-eliminate-water-scarcity/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 2021, he co-founded a second startup, H2MOF, which applies his discoveries in reticular chemistry to address challenges in [[hydrogen storage]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Meredith |first=Sam |date=2024-02-15 |title='The holy grail': Startup backed by a Nobel laureate vying for a breakthrough on hydrogen storage |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2024/02/15/nobel-laureate-hopes-startup-can-achieve-hydrogen-storage-breakthrough.html |access-date=2024-04-29 |website=CNBC }}</ref>

== Honors and awards ==
[[File:Omar M. Yaghi, 2025 Nobel laurate in chemistry.jpg|thumb|right|200px|Yaghi in 2025 Nobel lecture]]
[[File:2025 Nobel laurates in chemistry autographed chair.jpg|thumb|right|200px|2025 Nobel laureates in chemistry autographed chair]]
[[File:2025 Nobel laurates in chemistry.jpg|thumb|right|200px|Yaghi with [[Susumu Kitagawa]]]]
Yaghi has received numerous international awards and medals, including the [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] (2025), the [[Albert Einstein World Award of Science]] (2017), the [[Wolf Prize in Chemistry]] (2018), the [[Gregori Aminoff Prize]] (2019), the [[VinFuture Prize]] (2022), and the Science for the Future Ernest Solvay Prize (2024). His key honors include:

* 1998 Solid State Chemistry Award, [[American Chemical Society]] and [[Exxon|Exxon Co.]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=The ExxonMobil Award Faculty Fellowship in Solid State Chemistry |url=https://acsdic.org/awards/the-exxonmobil-award-faculty-fellowship-in-solid-state-chemistry/ |access-date=2024-05-10 |website=Division of Inorganic Chemistry |archive-date=2021-07-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210710092658/https://acsdic.org/awards/the-exxonmobil-award-faculty-fellowship-in-solid-state-chemistry/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>
